questions.q: What is the core mistake the lesson says underlies insecure output handling?
options: Using too many AI models in one application
Writing model prompts that are too short
Treating model output as trusted, well-formed content simply because it came from 'our AI'
Deploying AI features too slowly
questions.explain: The lesson identifies the core mistake as assuming output is safe because it came from the application's own AI, when it's exactly as untrusted as user input.

questions.q: Per the lesson, why is a model's output exactly as untrusted as user input?
options: Because all models are poorly engineered
Because output is always in a foreign language
Because an attacker who can influence what goes into the model, through a crafted prompt or injection, can influence what comes out
Because models always produce random, meaningless text
questions.explain: The lesson explains that attacker influence over input (via prompts, jailbreaks, or injection) carries through to the output if it isn't validated.

questions.q: Which of these is the SSRF (server-side request forgery) failure mode described in the lesson?
options: A server fetching a URL generated or extracted by the model, which could point at internal infrastructure
A user forgetting their password
A model taking too long to generate a response
A model's training run crashing partway through
questions.explain: The lesson describes SSRF as a server fetching a model-generated URL that could point anywhere, including internal systems.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say 'the model is usually right' is the wrong mental model for a security control?
options: Because models are never right about anything
Because security is about what a motivated attacker can make happen in the uncommon case, not the average case
Because this framing is only relevant to pricing decisions
Because it correctly describes how security controls should be evaluated
questions.explain: The lesson argues a control that only needs to fail once to cause damage must be evaluated against the worst case an attacker can induce, not the common case.

questions.q: What is the shared defense pattern the lesson recommends for closing most of these failure modes at once?
options: Disabling the AI feature entirely
Hiring more customer support staff
Treat model output exactly like input from an anonymous user, applying the same escaping, sandboxing, and parameterization controls
Increasing the model's temperature setting
questions.explain: The lesson's defense pattern is to apply the same validation, escaping, sandboxing, and parameterization controls already used for untrusted user input.
